# Part I: What I’m Trying to Create #

## 1. What a Good Game Looks Like to Me ##

### What I Want Players to Experience ###

I want the game to feel like a good carnival ride: adrenaline, exhaustion, excitement, and real emotion. I want everyone at the table to have a good time.

My biggest sign that a game has worked is what the players do when it ends. Either they don't want to leave, or they leave rehashing what happened. That energy—the desire to stay in the experience or to keep talking about it afterward—is what I look for.

#### I Design Systems, Not Stories ####

I build a world with enough pressure and meaning for the players' choices, the forces' actions, and the Stage's tensions to create the story in play.

### What Makes a Session Feel Successful ###

A session is successful when the players are engaged enough to want more, or when the events keep mattering to them afterward. It can feel cohesive even when the characters surprise me and change the situation.

### What I Prioritize When I Can't Have Everything ###

The table's fun is the only thing I will not sacrifice. Everything else can give way: the plot, the characters, the NPCs, the current TTRPG system, and more.

If the dice are getting in the way, I throw them out and play make-believe instead. Whatever works for the table is more important than continuing to use a rule or tool that is making the game less fun.

### What I'm Comfortable Leaving Out ###

I'm comfortable leaving out or changing anything that gets in the way of the table's fun. I don't need to preserve a planned plot, protect an NPC from the consequences of play, or keep using a system just because we started with it.

This doesn't mean I don't care about continuity, characters, or the story. I use preparation and the campaign's forces to help keep events coherent while improvising. But those are ways to support the experience, not obligations that outrank it.

## 2. The GM's Job—and Its Limits ##

### What I Take Responsibility For ###

I technically have authority over the forces and the world's reactions, but I don't think of myself as standing above the table. I think of myself as its steward. My job is to help create and maintain a situation the table can enjoy, and to respond to what happens without forcing the game down a predetermined path.

That includes making calls in the moment. I use the forces, their goals and limits, and what has already happened to make the world's responses feel like they belong. I also take responsibility for making the game safe enough for everyone at the table to participate.

### What I Leave to the Players ###

I don't try to predict what the characters will do or require them to follow a planned sequence. The players decide what their characters attempt, and those choices can change the campaign.

### What We Decide Together ###

Safety is the ultimate authority at my table. As a group, we decide what can initially go into the game and when it can happen. During play, every player has veto power over content, no questions asked. This is my one hard rule.

When someone uses a veto, the offending context is removed. The practical steps I use to establish and honor this boundary are in Chapter 4.

The table's fun is shared, too. I am a member of the table, and my enjoyment matters as much as any one player's. I find enjoyment in doing something well, so I'm willing to throw out the plot, characters, NPCs, or even the system if that is what the table needs. I recommend that prospective GMs figure out what makes GMing enjoyable for them and find a group that wants that kind of game. I usually ask my players to help us find our fun together. If we can't, I end the game; if one person at the table isn't having fun, it tends to tank the whole table.

### How Authority Works at My Table ###

My authority over the forces and the world's reactions is practical, not absolute. I use it in service of the table, never to overrule a safety veto or protect a planned story. If there is a conflict about a rule or ruling, I bring it to a table vote and move on. My approach to ordinary rules questions is covered in [Making Decisions in the Moment](./part-iii.md#8-making-decisions-in-the-moment).

## 3. The Principles Behind My Decisions ##

### My Core Principles ###

#### Safety is the hard boundary ####

The table decides what content is acceptable, and every player can veto content at any time without explanation. Nothing about a plot, encounter, or character takes priority over that.

#### The table's fun comes first ####

The table's fun is the one thing I will not sacrifice. Plot, characters, NPCs, and even the game system are all things I can change or discard if they get in the way. I am part of the table, too, so I look for a kind of play we can enjoy together.

#### Theme gives the campaign meaning ####

Theme is the question or idea the campaign keeps putting into play. I develop the Stage, Forces, their collisions, and the fallout so that, together, they let the characters encounter it from different angles. When deciding what happens next, I first ask, “What is the most interesting outcome that can happen within the theme?” Then I work out how the established situation can bring it about. No single detail has to represent the theme; the campaign's parts create opportunities to explore it through play. The characters' choices let us see what the question means to them. I do not use theme to dictate a lesson or decide the answer. Safety, the table's fun, and the players' freedom to choose remain essential.

#### Prepare situations, not outcomes ####

I put substantial effort into the initial campaign concepts, especially the forces: what they want, what they will and will not do, and how their actions can be recognized. I use this preparation to understand the situation, not to predict what the characters will do or dictate what must happen.

Theme guides that preparation by giving it a question to explore. I use it to shape the Stage, the forces and their goals, their fingerprints, and the conflicts their actions create, so their details work together to raise that question in play. It does not prescribe what the characters must do or believe.

#### Let play change the situation ####

The characters' actions matter. Forces pursue their goals, react to interference, and may change as the campaign develops. I follow what the table finds engaging rather than insisting that players pursue every prepared thread.

#### Preserve the Appearance of Continuity ####

Continuity is not important for its own sake; what matters is its appearance. I want events and character actions to fit the players' understanding of the world and its theme, so that changes do not break that understanding or make the campaign's meaning feel arbitrary. I can engineer an explanation backward when needed. Often the players will make those connections for me, filling in how a new development fits what they already know.

There is a kind of magic in this. Players can experience the world as solid and complete, and the GM as an extraordinary planner, even when the GM is improvising. The goal is not to fool the players about what was prepared in advance. Like a magician creating a moment of wonder, I want us to share an experience that feels magical and memorable. The preparation gives me enough understanding to respond coherently; play supplies the unexpected connections.

#### Treat the GM as a steward ####

I technically decide how forces and the world react, but I think of myself as the table's steward, not as an authority standing outside it. My decisions should help the group have a good experience, not protect my plans from the players.

### How These Principles Affect Play ###

I prefer encounters to arise from the fallout of character actions rather than being inserted as separate events. In tactical games, I prepare spreads of enemies for different encounter types and reskin them to fit the situation that actually arises.

### When Principles Conflict ###

Safety is the hard boundary; within it, the table's fun comes first. Continuity helps players trust the world, but I will revise details rather than let literal consistency undermine player choice or enjoyment.

### Where My Approach Differs from Familiar Advice ###

The advice I have the biggest problem with is advice that starts by having the GM create encounters as separate units. Encounters are important, but I find they work better when they flow naturally from the fallout of character actions. That way, the encounter belongs to the developing situation instead of interrupting it.

This is more difficult in tactical games such as D&D, where encounters may need carefully composed enemy groups. Preparing adaptable enemy spreads lets me keep that tactical structure without deciding in advance when or why an encounter will occur.
